planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this miniature meadow-rue spreads gradually by rhizome to form a low mat.

directions: Plant in partial shade in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil; Dwarf Korean Meadow-Rue is a tiny, maidenhair-fern-like groundcover reaching only 4-6 inches tall, spreading by rhizomes to form an airy mat 12-18 inches wide. Fluffy lavender-pink flowers appear from June through August, floating just above the delicate, finely divided foliage. It is a choice woodland-garden or shaded rock-garden groundcover for a spot with consistent moisture, and divides easily in spring if a larger planting is wanted.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moist soil in partial shade to shade; this Lamiaceae woodlander blooms later than most shade perennials, extending seasonal interest into fall.

directions: Plant in partial shade to shade in humus-rich, consistently moist soil; Japanese Turtlehead is an erect mint-family perennial reaching 12-20 inches, bearing dusky purple-pink tubular flowers from July through October, well after most shade perennials have finished blooming for the season. This late bloom window makes it a valuable addition to extend a shaded border's display into fall. It is unrelated to the North American turtlehead (Chelone), sharing only a superficial flower resemblance and the common name.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in shade; Giant Liverleaf carries the largest foliage of any hepatica species and resents disturbance once established.

directions: Plant in shade in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil; Giant Liverleaf is a Korean island endemic from Ulleungdo, bearing the largest foliage of any hepatica species, with rounded three-lobed leaves up to 15 cm across. Early-spring flowers in white to pale pink open before the new leaves fully expand, a classic hepatica display on a notably larger scale than the already-common Hepatica nobilis and americana. Give it a permanent, undisturbed woodland-garden spot, since hepaticas are slow to establish and resent transplanting once settled.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich, moist soil in shade; Yabumyoga produces vivid blue berries in autumn after an inconspicuous late-summer bloom, a genuine fall highlight.

directions: Plant in shade in humus-rich, consistently moist soil; Yabumyoga is a Japanese woodland relative of dayflower with glossy, Aspidistra-like foliage reaching 12-24 inches, bearing white flower racemes in late summer followed by strikingly vivid blue berries in autumn. The berry display is the main ornamental draw, adding a genuinely unusual color to the fall shade garden. It is hardy to roughly -15°C (zone 7), and spreads gradually to form a modest colony in congenial conditions.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in deep shade; Chinese Tupistra is closely related to Rohdea and shares its tolerance for the darkest garden corners.

directions: Plant in deep shade in humus-rich, well-drained soil; Chinese Tupistra is a Rohdea relative forming a 1-2 foot evergreen mound of wide, ruffled strap leaves, grown chiefly for its bold, architectural foliage rather than its subtle basal flower spikes, which are easily hidden under the leaves. Like Rohdea it tolerates the darkest, driest corners of a garden better than almost any other broadleaf evergreen, needing minimal care beyond occasional cleanup of old leaves. It is a genuine specialty item best sourced from a dedicated shade-plant nursery.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring into well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade; Kakuremino grows slowly and is prized for its dramatically different juvenile and adult leaf shapes.

directions: Plant in shade to part sun in well-drained, humus-rich soil; Kakuremino is an evergreen shrub-to-small-tree in the Aralia family, slowly reaching 15-17 feet, with a striking heteroblastic leaf change from tri-lobed juvenile foliage to entire, rhombic adult leaves on the same plant. Inconspicuous green summer flowers give way to black berries in fall. Its name, meaning 'hiding-cloak,' references a legendary invisibility cape in Japanese folklore, evoking the dense evergreen cover the mature foliage provides. It grows slowly and is best as a long-term shade-garden specimen rather than a quick screening plant.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; seed needs cold stratification to germinate reliably, and this species is sourced mainly through specialty/seed-trade channels rather than potted retail.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in moist, well-drained soil; Spurless Columbine is a dainty East Asian relative of true columbine, bearing nodding pink-to-white miniature columbine-like flowers in spring, but lacking the characteristic spurs of Aquilegia. Known in Chinese traditional medicine as tian kui, it is mainly available through specialty seed-trade and hardy-plant-society sources rather than mainstream potted retail. It self-sows modestly in congenial woodland-edge conditions once established and adds an unusual, delicate accent to a shaded spring border.
